title: They finally had their dream food truck. Then it was repossessed
summary: A family ran their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of a food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia until RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing…

image.caption: Leonardo Illas Jr., his wife Dayarit Duarte, his mother Maylin Rodriguez and his father Leo Illas now work out of the arena in Oxford, N.S. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

A family ran their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of a food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia until RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing the vehicle.
Family business, LeoMay Fusion, found second-hand truck on Facebook Marketplace
While Maylin Rodriguez prepares lunch service in Oxford, N.S., she worries about how her family will repay a loan for a food truck it no longer has.

Rodriguez and her family had run their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of the food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia before RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing the second-hand vehicle.

"We were like, this can't be happening. We paid for this truck. We think that we did things properly. They just let us know that the person who sold it to us had no right to sell the truck,” she said.
“We were devastated. Still in this disbelief.”

Rodriguez and her husband, son and daughter-in-law now serve customers out of the canteen in the community’s arena. They are open seven days a week, trying to repay the approximately $65,000 they borrowed to buy the truck, outfit it and get the business up and running.
The family travelled to Quebec to buy the truck and then operated for about a year after upgrading it. (LeoMay Food Truck/Facebook)
But they say their sales at the canteen are less than 10 per cent of what they earned serving dishes inspired by their Cuban and Venezuelan roots at events around the region.

They bought the food truck in Quebec after connecting with a seller on Facebook Marketplace. From the start, they said, it didn’t operate as promised and they had to upgrade the water system and deep fryer.

The family, who came to Canada in the past decade, said they had a steep learning curve — from figuring out how to do the accounting and taxes to sourcing the food and cooking quality meals quickly. They did plenty of research and asked other businesses for advice, said Leonardo Illas Jr., Rodriguez’s son.
"At first it was just a dream, then working toward getting things going, then suddenly you're there and it's fantastic but it's definitely challenging,” he said.
The family that operates LeoMay Fusion took their food truck to events across Nova Scotia and to other parts of the Maritimes. (Submitted by LeoMay Fusion)
It was a dream that ended abruptly when they learned there was a lien against the truck in Quebec. It wasn’t caught when they registered the vehicle in Nova Scotia.
Now the family wants to warn others to take precautions when buying second-hand goods.
Up to purchaser to search for liens

Lenders and some companies, like garages, can place liens on a vehicle, allowing them to repossess it if debts go unpaid. Liens can also be applied to mobile homes, boats, off-road vehicles and tractors.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre said in a statement it’s important for buyers to do due diligence, including verifying a seller’s information, confirming ownership and checking for outstanding liens or financial claims.

Rodriguez said they took their bill of sale to the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec, which handles vehicle registration in Quebec, and were told they could proceed with registering it in Nova Scotia. She said no one mentioned checking for liens there or when they registered it.
The Nova Scotia Registry of Motor Vehicles requires a certificate signed from a past owner, but it is not responsible for checking for liens, a spokesperson told CBC News.
There is a site that for a fee searches for liens across the territories and Atlantic Canada using a vehicle’s identification number (VIN). Quebec and other provinces have separate systems.
Leonardo Illas Jr., left, says his father Leo Illas Sr., right, has been applying to jobs. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

Dealerships are responsible for checking for liens before they sell used vehicles, but the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada warns that the rules around whether private sellers must disclose liens vary by province. It advises people to check for liens themselves through online personal property searches.
Rodriguez said her family didn’t know the right questions to ask and learned too late about the importance of checking for liens.
“What about new Canadians, newcomers, young people that don't know and they want to … [be] entrepreneurs? It would be great if they can have some guidance,” said Rodriguez.
“We come here, we learn English, we learn new rules, but we can't learn [it] all. And I think the institutions should offer as much information as they can so we can be prepared."
Considering legal action
Rodriguez said they’ve shared all the documentation they have with police in Longueuil, Que. The force said it is reviewing the incident and there have been no criminal charges.

RCMP in Nova Scotia declined to comment as they are not the lead agency. Their only involvement was being there as a safety precaution when the truck was repossessed, and a spokesperson said lenders often ask for their presence.
Meanwhile, the family is still on the hook for the money they borrowed. They said they’ve consulted a lawyer in Quebec but don’t know if they can afford to take any legal action.

The Cumberland branch of the Community Business Development Corporation, which issued their loan, said in a statement that they “recognize the difficult circumstances facing the business owners,” but declined to comment on the case.

Maylin Rodriguez, who is originally from Cuba, hopes lenders and other organizations consider that newcomers don't always know the right questions to ask when starting businesses. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)
The LeoMay Fusion team had hoped to operate the canteen and food truck concurrently this winter. Instead, they had to cancel commitments to community groups, who they thanked for being understanding.
“We served large events. We had the whole season scheduled, so we were counting on that revenue. But then [we] changed to here,” Rodriguez said at the canteen.
“We've seen a significant drop in our earnings, which is understandable because it's a small town.”
'Heartbreaking to hear what happened'

Ongoing repairs at the Oxford rink mean there is currently no ice surface, resulting in slower days at the canteen. The family said they’ve been grateful for the support of loyal customers like Emme Bidwell, who stopped in on Monday, picking up a chicken and pork rice bowl.
“It’s one of my favourite meals,” Bidwell said. "It's just heartbreaking to hear what happened. But anything we can do to support our local small restaurants."
LeoMay Fusion has a takeout window in the arena in Oxford, N.S. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)
Illas already works a second job. His father is looking for one.
“It's been a lot — having to apply for jobs, having to deal with lawyers, having to deal with the police … cancelling events,” said Illas.
Rodriguez said she understands they may never get their money back, and hopes lenders and other organizations consider their story and ways to better support other newcomers.

blocks.text: “Of course we want justice for our family. We would like to recover what we lost," she said.

"But if we can prevent someone else, another family, newcomer, new Canadian, someone trying to build a business, to go through the same pain that we're going [through], then speaking publicly is worth it,” added Rodriguez.

Elizabeth McMillan is a journalist with CBC in Halifax. For more than 15 years, she has reported from the edge of the Arctic Ocean to the Atlantic Coast and loves sharing people's stories. You can send tips and feedback to elizabeth.mcmillan@cbc.ca.
